title: DFS Documented Ties Between the Far-Right Knights of Columbus and the PAN
author: Fernanda Monroy
content:
_This article by[Fernanda
Monroy](https://contralinea.com.mx/author/fermonroy/) originally appeared in
the [September 3, 2026 edition of
Contralínea](https://contralinea.com.mx/investigacion/dfs-documento-vinculo-
del-grupo-ultraderechista-caballeros-de-colon-con-el-pan/), one of Mexico’s
leading investigative magazines._

![Declassified DFS document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/dfs-caballeros-colon-folder.jpg)The DFS master file on
the Knights of Columbus: box 16, file one. Photo: Contralínea

Part Four. A historic opponent of progressive agendas and of the sexual and
reproductive rights of women and the LGBT+ community, the far-right
organization Knights of Columbus (Caballeros de Colón) has associated not only
with right-wing parties but also with conservative pressure groups, such as
the National Catholic Association of Parents and Mexican Catholic Action.
Sheltered under the country’s most reactionary Catholic banner, their ideas
are linked to anti-communism.

**For more than three decades, the Knights of Columbus** —an organization
founded in the United States in the late 19th century and with an
international presence—**built in Mexico a network that linked members of the
National Action Party (PAN) with businessmen, Catholic hierarchs, and foreign
leaders**.

**The file that the Federal Security Directorate (DFS) compiled on this
group** —kept among its master copies, in box 16, file one—**shows that its
members’ activities went beyond charity and religious formation** : they took
part in electoral campaigns, educational disputes, debates over national
history, and dealings tied to bilateral affairs.

One of those connections was recorded in May 1962, when nearly 1,000 members
of the Order arrived in Chihuahua to hold their national convention in the
auditorium of a Pepsi-Cola bottling plant. A few blocks away, from the PAN’s
offices, propaganda was being printed and youth brigades and “lightning
rallies” were being organized in favor of **Cipriano Rubio Domínguez** , the
PAN candidate in the July local elections. DFS agents followed both activities
and placed young people linked to the Knights of Columbus within the electoral
brigades, although their reports did not specify whether an institutional
agreement existed between the Order and the party.

The organization then had a reach that extended beyond Mexico’s borders. A
March 1961 record described it as a fraternal structure divided into **63
jurisdictions** , with **approximately 1.2 million members and 4,200
councils** around the world. According to the document, its members were
selected for their integrity, loyalty to the Church, and willingness to fight
“for God, for the Church itself, and for the homeland.”

The files were produced by the political police of an authoritarian PRI regime
that surveilled and persecuted students, unions, campesinos, opponents, and
religious organizations.

In one of the files, the DFS reconstructed the scope of **an organized
Catholic right** , with national and international resources and connections,
that sought to influence politics, education, public morality, and the
decisions of the State. Today, the Knights of Columbus state that in Mexico
they have 18,250 local councils.

![Declassified DFS document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/dfs-caballeros-colon-report-1.jpg)A June 29, 1961 DFS
report describing the Knights of Columbus as “one of the most powerful groups
the clergy has.” Photo: Contralínea

## The Links to Acción Nacional

The files of the defunct “political police” document the presence of leaders
and militants of Acción Nacional in spaces shared with the Order and other
traditionalist organizations. Those gatherings show that religious militancy
and party participation converged around a common agenda: to expand the
political influence of Catholicism and to combat some of the foundations of
the secular State.

One of those convergences was recorded in September 1971, during a tribute to
**Agustín de Iturbide** held before **some 1,100 people** at the Cine Teatro
Metropólitan in Mexico City. Taking part in the event were members of the
Knights of Columbus, **the Mexican Traditionalist Movement** , the **Bernardo
Bergöend** Group, and militants of Acción Nacional.

Among the speakers was **Edmundo Gurza** , a member of the traditionalist
group and a regional PAN leader in Torreón, Coahuila, who accused “Masonic
governments” of altering Mexico’s history to suit their interests.

At the same gathering, the historian **Celerino Salmerón** denied Vicente
Guerrero’s participation in drafting the Plan of Iguala and called for
combating what he defined as an “intellectual system of lies established in
Mexico.” The vindication of Iturbide over Guerrero, José María Morelos,
Valentín Gómez Farías, and Benito Juárez was not merely a dispute about the
past; it confronted the liberal tradition that underpinned the separation of
Church and State.

The DFS reported attendance at the ceremony in memory of Iturbide at around
600 people, and identified among the leading figures **José González Torres**
, former national president of the PAN and one of the most visible Catholic
leaders within the party. Other documents included in the files show that
ecclesiastical sectors were calling for people not to support the political
forces that defended the provisions of the 1917 Constitution deemed by the
Church to be “persecutory.”

Taken together, the documents show a political community in which leaders and
militants shared events, adversaries, and objectives. Within that network,
**the PAN appears as the most visible partisan channel** for sectors of the
Catholic right that sought to recover influence over education, the
interpretation of history, and the decisions of the State.

![Declassified DFS document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/dfs-caballeros-colon-report-2.jpg)The DFS report
details the Order’s aims, methods, and Mexican membership. Photo: Contralínea

## A National Network With International Connections

The influence of the Knights of Columbus rested on a territorial structure
made up of professionals, businessmen, political leaders, and members of the
Catholic hierarchy. According to the DFS reports, the Order grew **from around
8,000 members in 1964 to 10,000 in 1966** , spread across more than a hundred
councils. The directories included in the files identified local
representatives—called Grand Knights—in more than 60 towns across the country.

In the leadership, **José Cárdenas Stille** stood out, identified as supreme
director of the Knights of Columbus in Mexico and as **the first Mexican to
hold one of the 21 posts in the worldwide leadership**. In Guadalajara there
also appeared **Adolfo Rojas** , registered as Grand Knight and head of the
local organization. These appointments show a structure that linked the
regional councils with the national leadership and, in turn, with the
international governance of the Order.

The organization gathered resources through individual contributions and
directed them to schools, universities, scholarships, literacy campaigns, and
aid for priests. It also had access to business, religious, and governmental
spaces. At its **1964 Acapulco convention** it brought together **nearly 2,000
delegates** , along with Catholic hierarchs and international leaders; the
closing was headed by former president **Miguel Alemán Valdés** , then head of
the National Tourism Council.

The presence of Alemán Valdés shows that the relationship with the PRI regime
was not one of permanent confrontation, despite the DFS’s surveillance. The
Order also maintained dialogue with foreign representatives. During the 1965
visit to Mexico of **John McDevitt** —an international leader known as the
Supreme Knight—agents recorded the attendance of **the ambassadors of the
United States, Canada, and the Philippines, as well as the Vatican’s apostolic
delegate**.

Its membership in a structure headed from the United States broadened that
capacity for action. This allowed the Knights of Columbus to mobilize
resources and carry Mexican matters into foreign political arenas, as happened
during the crisis caused by the salinity of **the Colorado River** , which
damaged agriculture in the Mexicali Valley and generated a bilateral conflict
during the 1960s.

The problem worsened from 1961, when the farmers of the **Wellton-Mohawk**
district in Arizona built a system of **94 deep wells** to extract brackish
water from the subsoil and reclaim their own lands. The drainage liquid was
discharged into the Colorado River before it crossed the border at the Morelos
Dam. As a result, the salinity of the water used by Mexican farmers rose from
around 900 parts per million to levels exceeding **2,700 parts per million**.

According to the reports included in the file, the flow deposited more than
**5,000 tons of salt** daily in the Mexicali Valley and affected an area
estimated at 450,000 acres, equivalent to around 182,000 hectares. The loss of
productivity left hundreds of farmers without harvests, access to credit, or
sufficient means of subsistence.

The conflict also opened a dispute over the interpretation of the **1944 Water
Treaty**. The United States maintained that the volume allocated to Mexico had
to be delivered regardless of its origin, while the Mexican government argued
that the water had to be suitable for agricultural and municipal uses. Mexico
further questioned whether drainage artificially extracted from wells in
Arizona could be counted as part of the natural flow of the Colorado River.

The DFS recorded the fear that left-wing organizations—among them the
**Independent Campesino Central** —would capitalize on the discontent of the
ejidatarios and call for protests in front of the **United States Consulate**.

In response, the Knights of Columbus incorporated the conflict into their
agenda after discussing it at the national convention in Acapulco. The
representative for Baja California, **Marín Vázquez Gudiño** , brought the
problem to the international assembly held on **August 20, 1964, in New
Orleans** , where the delegates approved the creation of a special commission
to travel to Washington and request a meeting with President **Lyndon B.
Johnson**.

The documents attest to the approval of the commission, although they do not
confirm whether its members managed to meet with Johnson or what results the
effort produced. Even with that caveat, the episode shows how the Mexican
representation could activate the Order’s U.S. structure and seek access to
the **White House** to influence a bilateral matter.

The initiative reveals the existence of a channel of influence parallel to
official diplomacy, sustained by relationships built on both sides of the
border. The power of the Knights of Columbus did not come from a mass
membership comparable to the PRI’s labor and campesino federations, but from
the combination of private resources, internal discipline, and access to
companies, dioceses, parties, diplomats, and foreign authorities.

![Declassified DFS document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/dfs-caballeros-colon-report-3.jpg)The report, signed
by DFS director Colonel Manuel Rangel Escamilla. Photo: Contralínea

## The Conservative Agenda That Remains in Force

The structure of the Knights of Columbus also served to promote an agenda that
went beyond religious ceremonies and charitable works. Their positions covered
education, the interpretation of national history, the content broadcast by
the media, and, later, sexual, reproductive, and identity rights.

One of their main areas of dispute was education. The files recorded the
rejection by the Order and other ecclesiastical sectors of the secular
provisions of **Article 3 of the Constitution**. That opposition was part of a
broader conflict against the liberal tradition that underpinned the separation
of Church and State.

During the 1960s, the agenda extended to cinema, radio, and television. The
Knights of Columbus took part in campaigns against what they called
“pornography” and “immorality,” under the idea that **Catholics had to
intervene in politics to steer it according to their principles**. In the
following decades, their spokesmen also came out against the legalization of
abortion and artificial birth control.

That agenda retains expressions in the present, since on **June 25, 2026** ,
the **Edelmiro Traslosheros Assembly 416 of the Knights of Columbus** came out
against the reform aimed at ensuring that girls, boys, and adolescents can
obtain a birth certificate consistent with their self-perceived gender
identity. The group asked the **Congress of Puebla** not to approve the
amendment, even though it stemmed from a ruling by the Supreme Court of
Justice of the Nation that declared it unconstitutional to absolutely exclude
minors from that procedure.

The forms of intervention have changed, but a recognizable ideological core
remains: the defense of a traditional conception of the family, religious
participation in legislative debates, and opposition to the expansion of
rights related to sexuality, reproduction, and identity. The position taken in
Puebla shows that this agenda was not confined to the files that the DFS
compiled, but continues to move into the legislatures and legal disputes of
the present.

![Declassified DFS document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/dfs-caballeros-colon-oath-1.jpg)The “Fourth Degree
Oath” transcribed in the DFS file. Photo: Contralínea

## Surveillance From Power

The files cannot be separated from the institution that produced them. **The
DFS acted as the political police of an authoritarian PRI regime** and, in the
case of the Knights of Columbus, its reports reveal assessments produced in
the midst of confrontation with an organization connected to PAN members.

That tension appears in a report dated **June 29, 1961** , signed by the
director of the DFS, **Manuel Rangel Escamilla**. The document described the
Knights of Columbus as “one of the most powerful groups the clergy has” and
attributed to it the ability to mobilize or “unify” nearly half a million
Catholics in Mexico to finance schools, universities, scholarships, and
religious propaganda.

The report noted that the Knights of Columbus could not be considered a secret
society and that its statutes prohibited introducing politics within the
Order, under penalties for those who violated that provision. **At the same
time, it acknowledged that its members were free to fulfill their “civic
duties,”** which left open the possibility of combining religious membership
with political participation on an individual basis.

The DFS paid special attention to its mechanisms of internal formation.
According to the report, the Order held **a ritual reserved “for psychological
reasons,”** whose “sober” and “highly meaningful” character functioned as a
means of attraction and cohesion. Formation advanced through different degrees
and drew on symbols and emblems to fix the organization’s principles in the
initiates until they became, according to the report, a “second nature”
capable of producing “notable changes in a man’s life.” At the same time, the
document noted that participation was voluntary and that the authorities used
fraternal means, without recording mechanisms of coercion.

The file also contains a text presented as the **“Fourth Degree Oath,”** which
attributed to the Order’s members the intention of **combating Masons and
Protestants, disobeying governments deemed hostile to the Church, and obeying
their superiors’ orders without question**. At the end, it stated that the
initiate had to sign the oath with his name, written with the tip of a dagger
“dipped in my own blood.”

The organization itself and U.S. authorities **denied that the text was
authentic**. However, those denials do not fully resolve the doubts about the
document either. The same is true of the fact that the DFS preserved and
transcribed it: **its appearance in their archives does not prove that the
oath was pronounced or that the described ceremony actually took place**. The
file leaves open questions about its origin and provides no testimony from
those who would have participated, authenticated internal documents, or other
elements that would allow confirmation of what is recounted there.

The political context of the era also requires **reading the document with
caution**. The DFS watched with suspicion an organization linked to sectors of
the PAN opposition, so that confrontation may have influenced the way it
interpreted their reserved practices. But there are also no grounds to assert
that the text was deliberately invented or altered.

**What the available documents do show is that the alleged oath was part of
the information the political police gathered and used to assess the Knights
of Columbus.** Even the agent who made the transcription avoided asserting
that it was authentic and closed the document with a phrase that passed that
judgment on to the reader: “We leave it to the reader’s judgment to make the
comments that his conscience dictates.”

The authenticity of the text remains unproven because the file contains no
direct testimony, authenticated internal documents, or other elements that
would allow one to affirm that **the oath was pronounced or that the described
rites were practiced by the Order**. Nevertheless, the archives do offer
evidence of another dimension of the Knights of Columbus: conventions,
directories, speeches, participants, and political relationships that make it
possible to reconstruct part of their activity in Mexico.

The files on the religious organization attest to an organized Catholic right,
articulated through local councils, private resources, international
relationships, and the ties of some of its members to the PAN.
